title: What is the difference between @MappedSuperclass and @Inheritance in JPA? When do you use shared fields versus a real polymorphic type hierarchy?
keyPoints: @MappedSuperclass shares columns with subclass entities but is not an entity itself -- no table, no polymorphic queries
@Inheritance makes a real entity hierarchy with polymorphic queries, associations, and its own table(s)
Use @MappedSuperclass purely to avoid repeating common fields like createdAt, updatedAt, and version
Use @Inheritance when subtypes are genuinely different kinds of the same thing you query polymorphically
@MappedSuperclass supports @PrePersist and @PreUpdate callbacks that all subclasses inherit
You can combine both: @MappedSuperclass for audit fields above an @Inheritance hierarchy for real types
Choosing @Inheritance forces a second decision about the strategy: SINGLE_TABLE, JOINED, or TABLE_PER_CLASS

s1_definition.oneliner: @MappedSuperclass shares columns with subclasses but is not an entity and cannot be queried; @Inheritance creates a real entity hierarchy with polymorphic queries and associations.
s1_definition.profdef:
JPA provides two mechanisms for class hierarchies, and they serve different purposes.

- **@MappedSuperclass** – a non-entity base class that holds shared mapping information (columns, audit fields) which subclass entities inherit as their own columns, but it has no table, no identity of its own, and cannot be queried or referenced polymorphically.
- **@Inheritance** – marks a base class that is itself an @Entity, creating a real type hierarchy where the base and all subclasses are entities that support polymorphic queries and polymorphic associations.
- **Polymorphic query** – a JPQL query against the base type that returns all subtypes, such as `SELECT a FROM Account a` returning both SavingsAccount and CurrentAccount rows.
- **@PrePersist / @PreUpdate** – lifecycle callbacks that a @MappedSuperclass can define once and all subclasses inherit, commonly used for automatic audit stamping.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, every form -- whether it is a savings form, a current-account form, or a loan form -- has a standard header block with the date, the branch code, and the officer's name. That header is like @MappedSuperclass: it is copied onto every form, but you cannot walk into the records room and ask "show me all headers" because a header is not a real form on its own. Now consider "Account" itself: Savings Account and Current Account are real kinds of Account, and you can ask the records room "give me all accounts" and receive both. That is @Inheritance: Account genuinely exists as a queryable category.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  @MappedSuperclass (not an entity, no table)

  Auditable
  ├── createdAt
  ├── updatedAt
  └── version
        │ inherits columns
        ├──────────────────────┐
        ▼                      ▼
  ┌─────────────┐       ┌──────────────────┐
  │ accounts    │       │ loan_applications│
  │ table       │       │ table            │
  ├─────────────┤       ├──────────────────┤
  │ account_id  │       │ loan_id          │
  │ holder_name │       │ applicant_name   │
  │ balance     │       │ loan_amount      │
  │ created_at  │       │ created_at       │
  │ updated_at  │       │ updated_at       │
  │ version     │       │ version          │
  └─────────────┘       └──────────────────┘
  (independent tables, no shared base table)
```

```text
  @Inheritance (base IS an entity, shared hierarchy)

  Account (entity, table = accounts)
  ├── account_id (PK)
  ├── holder_name
  ├── balance
  ├── account_type (discriminator)
        │
        ├── SAVINGS ──▶ SavingsAccount
        │                 └── interest_rate
        │
        └── CURRENT ──▶ CurrentAccount
                          └── overdraft_limit

  SELECT a FROM Account a
  → returns BOTH SavingsAccount and CurrentAccount rows
```

```text
  Combined pattern (production):

  @MappedSuperclass Auditable
  ├── createdAt, updatedAt, version
        │
        ▼
  @Entity @Inheritance Account
  ├── accountId, holderName, balance
        │
        ├── SavingsAccount (interestRate)
        └── CurrentAccount (overdraftLimit)

  Audit fields inherited + polymorphic queries work
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A @MappedSuperclass is a non-entity base class that holds shared mapping information like audit columns, a version field, and lifecycle callbacks. Each entity subclass inherits those fields as columns in its own table, but the base class has no table, no identity, and cannot be queried or referenced in relationships. It is purely a code-reuse mechanism to avoid duplicating common mappings across unrelated entities like Account, LoanApplication, and Customer.

@Inheritance creates a real entity hierarchy where the base class is itself an entity. SavingsAccount and CurrentAccount are genuinely different kinds of Account, and you can write a JPQL query against Account and get both subtypes back in one result. You can also have a @ManyToOne reference to Account that holds either subtype at runtime. This is what you need when the subtypes are real variants of the same domain concept that you sometimes treat uniformly and sometimes specifically.

At National Bank of India, Pankaj combines both mechanisms. A @MappedSuperclass called BaseEntity holds createdAt, updatedAt, and version with @PrePersist callbacks that stamp them automatically, and every entity in the system extends it. Separately, Account is a real @Inheritance hierarchy with SavingsAccount and CurrentAccount subtypes, because reporting needs to list all accounts together and transactions need to reference Account polymorphically. The two mechanisms combine naturally: BaseEntity for audit fields at the top, and Account for the real domain hierarchy below it.

Remember one sentence: @MappedSuperclass shares columns without being an entity; @Inheritance creates a real entity hierarchy you can query and associate polymorphically.
